meta.subtitle: Electrical connection and protection maker growing fast on infrastructure and data-center demand; the share price already reflects most of it.

analystCommentary: We rate nVent Electric HOLD with a $160 to $205 target range. Second-quarter 2026 sales rose by about half year over year, mostly organically. We do not doubt the growth; the question is what the shares already pay for it. Our scenarios put the probability-weighted value only a little above the price, while a stall in earnings would take the shares well below it. That asymmetry, not the operating record, sets the call, and the valuation section shows what would change it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: nVent Electric plc designs, manufactures, markets, installs and services electrical connection and protection solutions. It was founded in 1903 and is based in London, the United Kingdom. It reports two segments, Systems Protection and Electrical Connections, which represented approximately 72% and 28% of total revenues in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Its brands include nVent CADDY, ERICO, HOFFMAN, ILSCO, SCHROFF and TRACHTE, and its products serve industrial, commercial and residential, infrastructure and energy applications, including data centers. The portfolio changed in 2025. On January 30, 2025 nVent sold its Thermal Management business to an affiliate of funds managed by Brookfield Asset Management for $1.6 billion in net cash proceeds, subject to customary purchase price adjustments; that business is now reported as discontinued operations. On May 1, 2025 it bought the enclosures, switchgear and bus systems businesses of Avail Infrastructure Solutions, the Electrical Products Group, for approximately $1.0 billion, funded with cash on hand and operated predominantly within Systems Protection. FY25 revenue was $3.9 billion.

thesis.body: Management says the electrification, sustainability and digitalization megatrends, including the increased use of artificial intelligence, have led to sales growth, particularly in the infrastructure vertical that holds its data-center business, and it expects them to drive growth through 2026 and beyond. The second-quarter results bear that out: growth was mostly organic and operating margin widened. Two things hold us back. Gross margin fell even as sales rose, so the margin gain rests on the expense side and on volume staying high. And the price pays a full multiple for growth that consensus expects to slow. We think fair value sits only modestly above the price, with a deep downside if growth stalls, so the shares are a HOLD.

catalysts: Third-quarter 2026 results: with the acquisition closed in May 2025, its comparison effect should largely fall away and give a cleaner read on organic growth.
Data-center and power-utility demand: if the megatrends management cites continue, the infrastructure growth behind the second quarter should continue with them.
Operating margin: holding the second-quarter margin gain as the acquisition comparison fades would support our Base multiple.
risks: Valuation: a slowdown would cost multiple as well as earnings (see Valuation).
Growth concentration: a pause in data-center or utility spending would hit the business that drove most organic growth.
Gross-margin pressure: gross margin has fallen while sales rose.
Cash-flow basis: the statement table and the proxy disagree on FY25 cash flow, and the page cannot resolve the table's basis.
Cyclicality: the 10-K ties demand to the global economy, capital spending and interest rates.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter 2026 net sales were $1,471.3 million, {+ up 52.8% +} from $963.1 million a year earlier. Gross margin was 37.9%, {- down 0.7 points -} from 38.6%; the company attributes the decline to inflation in raw materials and labor, unfavorable product mix and investments in capacity, partly offset by volume leverage and productivity. Gross profit also included approximately $25 million of IEEPA tariff reimbursements, which the company says were offset by other incremental tariffs. SG&A fell 4.6 points as a share of sales, which the company credits to leverage on fixed expenses and restructuring savings, even as intangible amortization rose to $41.1 million from $35.9 million as a result of the acquisition. Operating income was $300.7 million, a 20.4% margin, {+ up 4.1 points +} from 16.3%. Net income from continuing operations rose 102.2% to $215.8 million, with the effective tax rate up to 23.5% from 22.7%, partly on $3.6 million of tax expense from a foreign tax audit settlement. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, net sales were $2,713.3 million, {+ up 53.1% +}, operating margin was 18.3% against 16.2%, and gross margin fell 1.7 points to 37.0%. Six-month net income fell 23.8% to $358.3 million because the prior-year half carried $276.5 million of discontinued-operations income, primarily the gain on the Thermal Management sale; income from continuing operations rose 83.9%. On the annual table, revenue grew in each of the last three years, by 29.5% in FY25, but gross margin fell to 37.7% from 40.2% in FY24 and operating margin to 15.8% from 17.5%; the page gives no explanation for the FY25 decline. Two sources disagree on FY25 EPS. The table shows diluted EPS of $4.31 on net income of $710.2 million and states no basis, while the proxy reports EPS from continuing operations of $2.60, up 82% from $1.43. The gap runs in the direction of the discontinued-operations income above. We use the proxy's figure, on the rule set out under cash flow.
financials.balanceCommentary: Total debt was $1.6 billion at FY25, down from $2.2 billion at FY24, against total equity of $3.7 billion. The table shows no cash or net-debt figure for FY24 or FY25, so the page cannot tell us how much of the Thermal Management proceeds remained after the acquisition, and we do not label the company net cash or net debt. The current ratio was 1.63 at FY25 and 1.80 on a trailing basis. Second-quarter net interest expense was $17.4 million against $17.6 million a year earlier, small beside the quarter's operating income. The page shows no interest-coverage or net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio, so our leverage read rests on the debt and equity figures alone, and on those figures the balance sheet does not constrain the growth plan.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Two sources disagree on FY25 cash flow. The statement table shows operating cash flow of $0.5 billion, against $0.6 billion in FY24, and free cash flow of $371.9 million after $93.3 million of capital expenditure, an FCF margin of 9.6% against 18.9% in FY24. The March 2026 proxy reports net cash provided by operating activities of $649 million and total Free Cash Flow of $561 million, and says its results are on a continuing-operations basis. The table states no basis. Our rule for both disagreements, EPS and cash flow, is to use the source that states a continuing-operations basis, because we are valuing the business nVent still owns. We therefore use the proxy's figures, noting that Free Cash Flow is the company's own measure. The table's FY25 decline may reflect a basis difference the page cannot resolve, so we do not treat it as an operating decline. nVent paid $253.1 million for share repurchases and $130.4 million in dividends in FY25, in line with the approximately $383 million the proxy says it returned to shareholders, and within the company's Free Cash Flow measure. With a dividend yield of 0.52%, the return case rests on earnings growth rather than cash returned.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $162.85 the shares trade at 44.4x trailing earnings, 26.9x trailing EV/EBITDA and 5.5x sales. The page labels its 31.7x forward multiple as next twelve months, but that figure matches the price over FY26E consensus EPS of $5.14, so we read it as the current-year multiple and use it as the like-for-like reference. The 25.1x on FY27E EPS of $6.48 is today's price over next year's earnings, not a multiple the shares will trade on a year out. The pack carries no peer multiples and no history of nVent's own multiple, so we judge the current-year multiple against growth alone. Consensus EPS rises by roughly a quarter between the two years while consensus revenue growth slows (see Growth). A current-year multiple well above next year's expected EPS growth, with that growth slowing, is full: it pays in advance for growth beyond FY27E that no figure on the page supports. The other reading is that consensus expects EPS to grow faster than revenue, and that first-half sales growth ran above the full-year consensus rate, so consensus already assumes a slower second half that results could beat. We call the multiple full rather than stretched. The Street is more bullish than we are: 16 of 17 analysts rate the shares Buy, with a $206.67 consensus target, a $210.00 median and a $136.00 to $240.00 range. The shares sit below the $184.64 52-week high and far above the $93.22 low, and no source on the page explains either move.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Organic growth stays strong after the acquisition comparison fades and operating margin keeps rising, so the shares hold today's 31.7x current-year multiple a year out. We apply 32x, that multiple rounded, to FY27E consensus EPS of $6.48, which puts the Bull next to the Street's consensus target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus FY27E EPS is delivered, but as revenue growth slows the market pays 28x on it, a modest compression from today's current-year multiple. Slipping gross margin and the end of the acquisition contribution argue against holding the multiple; organic growth this strong argues against a deeper cut.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Data-center spending cools, gross margin keeps falling and FY27E growth does not arrive, leaving earnings near FY26E consensus EPS of $5.14. We apply 20x, our judgment for earnings that have stopped growing: well below the 25.1x paid today for a year of growth that this case removes, but above a no-growth floor, because the business stays profitable and the stall is cyclical. The result sits within the shares' own 52-week range.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting Bull 25%, Base 50% and Bear 25% gives an expected upside of +3.3% and a bear-case downside of -36.9%, a reward/risk of 0.09×, which derives HOLD. The Base carries half the weight because it is where the consensus numbers point once growth slows. Bull and Bear carry equal weight because the evidence cuts both ways: strong organic growth and a wider operating margin on one side; falling gross margin, a fading acquisition contribution and management's expectation of continued cost inflation on the other. The label holds across a wide band. Moving ten points of weight from Bear to Bull, or holding the Base at today's current-year multiple, still leaves HOLD, because the deep Bear keeps reward/risk below the BUY bar. On the downside, a Base at 25x or ten points moved from Bull to Bear each leaves HOLD on its own; together they derive SELL. The $160 to $205 target range brackets the Base.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The pack shows a single reportable segment, but the 10-Q reports two, and we follow the 10-Q. Systems Protection, the larger by revenue, sells enclosures, liquid and air cooling, control buildings, switchgear systems and power distribution that protect electronics, systems and data in mission critical applications, including data centers; the company says its data-center business sits primarily in this segment, and the Electrical Products Group is operated predominantly within it. Electrical Connections sells bus systems, cable management, electrical connections and power connections across commercial and residential, infrastructure and industrial verticals, and the company says its offerings reduce installation time. The excerpt gives no segment sales or segment income, so we cannot say which segment drove the margin gain.

moatFactors.name: Brand portfolio
moatFactors.body: Some of nVent's brands have a history spanning over 100 years, according to the March 2026 proxy, and they support the reputation for quality and reliability that the 10-K lists among the bases of competition.

moatFactors.name: Installed position in critical applications
moatFactors.body: The 10-K lists technical expertise, timeliness of delivery and previous installation history alongside price as bases of competition. Where nVent's products protect mission critical equipment in data centers and infrastructure, an installation history can favor the incumbent on the next project, though the same 10-K says some competitors compete primarily on price, localized expertise and local relationships.

moatFactors.name: Scale and breadth
moatFactors.body: A portfolio running from enclosures and cooling to connections and switchgear lets nVent serve customers whose demand the 10-K calls often global in scope but localized in delivery. The same filing says nVent competes with thousands of smaller regional and local companies that may offer products produced at lower cost, so breadth helps on global accounts but does not shield local business from cheaper rivals.

moatFactors.name: Pricing
moatFactors.body: The company counts selective increases in selling prices within its organic growth, yet gross margin still fell in the second quarter and the six months. Pricing has not kept gross margin up, so we do not treat it as a strong defense yet.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. Of the four factors, the installed position in mission critical applications and the brands carry the most weight; breadth and pricing add little. Against them, the 10-K describes highly competitive, geographically diverse markets with large, well-established global rivals and possible new entrants, and it warns that economic downturns could push market participants to compete more aggressively on price. The demand tailwind behind recent growth is not a moat. If data-center spending slows, that price competition would weigh more heavily, and nothing on the page shows that the factors above would hold margin in that case.

points: Second-quarter 2026 growth split into 46.9 points organic, 5.4 points from the acquisition and 0.5 points from currency; for the six months the split was 41.2, 10.7 and 1.2 points.

The infrastructure business contributed approximately 44.0 points of second-quarter organic growth and commercial and residential approximately 2.0 points; the company says this includes selective increases in selling prices and growth in the data-centers business.
The Electrical Products Group added $51.6 million of second-quarter sales and $189.3 million in the six months.
Consensus expects FY26E revenue of $5.5 billion, up about 40%, then $6.4 billion in FY27E, a smaller step.

Management's 2026 objectives include growth through higher-growth verticals, new products and innovation, and global expansion, and it says investment in new products has contributed to sales growth; its acquisition plans are covered under capital allocation.

management.leadership: The March 2026 proxy names the 2025 executive team. Beth A. Wozniak is Chair and Chief Executive Officer. Gary Corona became Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer effective March 31, 2025, when Sara E. Zawoyski, the former CFO, became President of Systems Protection; Brian Coleman became President of Electrical Connections effective March 17, 2025. Lynnette Heath is Executive Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer, and Aravind Padmanabhan is Executive Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. The proxy describes the Spark management system, built on People, Growth, Lean, Digital and Velocity. The finance and segment leadership changed in early 2025, so the team's record in its current roles is short, though the organic growth since then is strong.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation in 2025 turned on the portfolio. The March 2026 proxy calls 2025 a continuation of its "portfolio transformation to a higher-growth electrical company". Of the two deals, the Electrical Products Group purchase is the one the page ties to infrastructure: the 10-Q says that business serves primarily the infrastructure vertical, including power utilities and data centers. Shareholder returns came second; the FY25 buybacks and dividends discussed under cash flow are small beside the company's market value. Management's 2026 objectives pair deploying capital strategically to drive growth and value creation with acquisitions and the integration of recent deals, so further acquisitions are likely to take priority over a higher payout. That suits a business growing this fast, but it adds integration risk and leaves holders relying on execution rather than yield.
management.governance: The source is the March 2026 proxy excerpt. All non-employee directors are independent, there is an independent Lead Director, and independent directors meet regularly without management present. The proxy cites over 99% average board meeting attendance, annual board and committee self-assessments, proxy access for director nominees, no poison pill, stock ownership requirements for officers and directors, and an insider trading policy with anti-hedging and anti-pledging provisions. The board oversees risks including artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. In its 2025 outreach nVent held calls with holders of approximately 12% of outstanding shares, measured on June 30, 2025 data. The Chair and Chief Executive Officer roles are combined, a structure the independent Lead Director partly offsets. The excerpt shows no red flags, but it carries no pay figures, so we do not judge executive compensation.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt sets stock ownership requirements for officers and directors but includes no ownership table, so we cannot state insider stakes or judge how closely management's interests track outside holders'.

idiosyncratic: Demand concentration: most second-quarter organic growth came from the infrastructure business, which holds the data-center business. A pause in data-center or power-utility capital spending would hit growth and the operating-margin gain that rests on volume.

Cost inflation: management expects inflationary cost increases, including impacts related to tariffs, to continue throughout 2026 and beyond, which it says could negatively impact its results, and gross margin is already falling.

Acquisition integration: the 10-Q's forward-looking statements name integrating the Electrical Products Group as a risk, and the 10-K warns that acquisitions can bring unforeseen liabilities, impairment charges and dilution; the further deals discussed under capital allocation would add to it.
risks.systemic: The 10-K ties demand to the overall strength of the global economy, industrial and governmental capital spending, interest rates, inflation, and energy and commodity prices, and notes that many industrial customers are cyclical. nVent sells across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, India, Africa and Asia Pacific, and the 10-Q names volatility in currency exchange rates, interest rates and commodity prices, military conflicts and rapid changes in global trade policy among the factors that could move its results. These pressures would hit the sector broadly, not nVent alone.

body: Our call is HOLD, with targets of $160 to $205. The operating story is strong, but the price already sits close to our probability-weighted value, and our Bear case shows how far the shares could fall if growth stalls.

On unchanged scenarios, a price roughly a tenth below today's would derive BUY, and a return toward the $184.64 52-week high would derive SELL. Beyond price, later quarters showing organic growth near the second-quarter pace after the acquisition comparison has gone, with gross margin stabilizing, would move us toward BUY by supporting today's current-year multiple and a lower weight on a stall. On our math that alone still leaves HOLD; a BUY would also need evidence that a stall would cost the shares less than our Bear assumes. We would move toward SELL if organic growth slows sharply while gross margin keeps falling, the combination our Bear case describes.
